cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Name Your Backers
cards.instruction: Get someone to reveal who supports their position, who authorized it, and who benefits from it.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. This roof proposal says 'we recommend.' Who's we?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Finance backed the cheaper tiles. I need your signature to order them.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Who authorized Finance to choose the tiles?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: The facilities director. Savings go into her office refurbishment.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Add her approval and that refurbishment to the proposal. Before I sign, can she explain the trade-off to our maintenance team?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 challenges anonymous we, A3 withholds quick signature for authorization details and A5 commands named benefit disclosure before signing, making gatekeeping status the inquiry tactic.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 Finance support prompts A3 authorization question; B4 director approval and benefit prompt A5 recorded disclosure and explanation. A3 stock decision sentence is awkward but not contradictory to withholding signature.

relationship.evidence: B2 has an order needing signature and B4 supplies the self-interested beneficiary, giving A concrete reasons to demand accountability.

heightening.evidence: B4 office benefit causes A5 to bring the maintenance team into a trade-off explanation before approval.

specificity.evidence: A1 roof tiles, B2 cost choice and B4 refurbishment show the policy and benefit; no exact prices are needed.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 asks the benefiting director to explain the trade-off to those maintaining the roof, earning pressure from B4 revelation.
